name: Preservation to personal survival
position: Conditional project argument skeleton; not a finding
conclusion: If both additional premises hold, H-S follows for the specified person.
objection: Information preservation can occur while the original subject ceases; duplicates expose the identity problem.
reply: Specify a subject-preserving relation rather than infer it from informational fidelity.

name: Endurance and enduring significance
position: Conditional project argument skeleton; not a finding
conclusion: The specified persistence contributes enduring significance under those normative premises.
objection: Duration alone need not increase value, and finite value may exist without persistence.
reply: Identify the particular value preserved, such as a relationship, and argue for its normative importance.

name: Conscious production to cosmic purpose
position: Conditional project argument skeleton; not a finding
conclusion: H-I holds for that specified end if the agency and intention premises are warranted.
objection: The occurrence of an outcome is also compatible with an unintended byproduct.
reply: State ends and discriminating consequences independently of the observations being explained.

name: Conscious foundation to moral authority
position: Conditional project argument skeleton; not a finding
conclusion: H-A follows only to the extent the normative relation establishes the specified obligations.
objection: Descriptive unity, causal origin, power, or reward can leave binding moral justification unexplained.
reply: Develop a defensible good-nature or relational grounding account and compare non-theistic value/reason/obligation accounts.

name: Physicalism operational comparison
position: M-T03-PH; project stipulation, not philosopher attribution
conclusion: Physical constitution is a viable comparator.
objection: Phenomenal character may remain unexplained.
reply: Identity or grounding need not be conceptually transparent.

name: Psychophysical laws operational comparison
position: M-T03-PL; project stipulation, not philosopher attribution
conclusion: A constrained law model is a viable comparator.
objection: Mappings may leave their central dependence brute.
reply: Apply the same explanatory stopping rules across models.

name: Panpsychism operational comparison
position: M-T03-PA; project stipulation, not philosopher attribution
conclusion: The constitutive proposal warrants comparison.
objection: Many subjects do not evidently constitute one subject.
reply: Specify and constrain a subject-constitution relation.

name: Dualism operational comparison
position: M-T03-DU; project stipulation, not philosopher attribution
conclusion: An explicit dualist model warrants comparison.
objection: Interaction may conflict with a complete physical causal account.
reply: Assess causal completeness and explicit interaction laws separately.

name: Idealism operational comparison
position: M-T03-ID; project stipulation, not philosopher attribution
conclusion: Conscious grounding warrants comparison.
objection: Experiential knowledge does not prove mental ontology.
reply: Offer an overall explanatory argument and perspective-individuation model.

name: Theism operational comparison
position: M-T03-TH; project stipulation, not philosopher attribution
conclusion: A specified intentional creator warrants comparison.
objection: Explanation alone does not identify mind, goodness or authority.
reply: Supply distinct agency and normative arguments; test specified ends against suffering and hiddenness.

name: Functional explanation and phenomenal target
conclusion: Further explanatory demand.

name: Knowledge/conceivability and modal bridge
conclusion: Conditional rejection of physicalism.
reply: A-T05-002 dilemma in report

name: Phenomenal concepts and property identity
conclusion: Epistemic difference need not refute identity.

name: Identity and explanatory standards
conclusion: No further causal connection follows.

name: Alexander’s brain-independence argument
position: Strongest conditional reconstruction, not endorsed conclusion
conclusion: Conditional support for H-B; no automatic H-S/H-T or deity inference
objection: A-T06-002: neither temporal alignment nor exclusion of all relevant processing is established.
reply: Defender appeals to profound impairment, different recovery phenomenology and corroborative detail rather than credentials alone.

name: Underdetermination and ordinary alternatives
position: Audit reconstruction with Shermer’s original challenge
conclusion: This packet does not identify a unique neural or non-neural cause
objection: A-T06-001: severe impairment and corroborated details could challenge a precisely specified brain-dependent account.
reply: Preserve corroborative reports and propose independently dated/timed tests; do not declare hallucination merely because it is possible.

name: Severe illness versus solely pharmacological coma
conclusion: Avoid both drug-only dismissal and inference from serious illness to complete brain inactivity
objection: Witness accounts are retrospective and contested.
reply: Published chart review strengthens severe-illness documentation but is not a continuous functional recording.

name: Conditional inference to brain independence
conclusion: These studies motivate discriminating tests but do not establish H-B in this packet.
objection: No concealed target success with established opportunity and no content-specific experience during measured absent processing are demonstrated.
reply: Incomplete measurements do not refute testimony or establish an ordinary explanation of each case.

name: Physiological and methodological countercase
position: Challenges inference to H-B without establishing physicalism
conclusion: Brain-dependent possibilities remain open; neither physicalism nor brain independence is settled.
objection: Generic possibilities do not explain each detailed recollection.
reply: AWARE II itself acknowledges alpha-coma ambiguity and that association does not establish causation; objective participant-level testing remains necessary.

name: Recurrence across records and cultural settings
position: Strongest conditional case for a shared experiential phenomenon
conclusion: The inspected records support investigating recurrent experiences with varied content; they do not identify a unique metaphysical cause.
objection: Shared human cognition, literary transmission, selection and coding can produce recurrence; no common clinical denominator or assured independent samples.
reply: Cultural differences do not refute every shared experiential or survival model, and these narratives predate modern NDE publicity; a constrained model must predict more than broad similarities.

name: Cultural, reporting and measurement countercase
position: Strongest countercase to invariance and direct survival inference
conclusion: Cultural and measurement effects remain serious alternatives; these data neither establish a purely cultural mechanism nor demonstrate a universal afterlife structure.
objection: A common experiential or afterlife reality could be interpreted differently by cultures; observational variation need not exhaust the phenomenon.
reply: That possibility is retained, but retrospective flexibility earns no distinctive predictive support without prospective constraints.

name: Causal neural contributions constrain embodied mind models
conclusion: Neural processes causally contribute to embodied perception and state functions in these tested contexts; models denying any such contribution are challenged.
objection: Interventions may alter access/reporting, distributed routing or a posited interface without proving how experience is constituted.
reply: An interface account must specify predictions for the observed content, site and state effects rather than merely accommodate them.

name: Neural dependence does not by itself settle ontology
conclusion: Results constrain embodied models without uniquely selecting physicalism or brain independence, or licensing survival claims from failures of a neural theory.
objection: An unspecified interface view can fit any data and lose predictive force against explicit neural mechanisms.
reply: Require prospective contrasting predictions; logical underdetermination does not make alternatives equally supported.

name: Mechanism and agency compatibility
conclusion: A mechanism alone does not exclude agency; positive support requires an additional comparison.
objection: Observed human artifact origins do not establish cosmic agency.
reply: Unobserved causes can be inferred; require a discriminatory reason rather than direct observation as an absolute rule.

name: Intelligibility and rational origin
conclusion: If these comparisons hold, intelligibility favors the specified rational-origin model.
objection: Agent preferences and contrast class may be fitted after observing the world; impersonal structure and learning may also explain fit.
reply: A common rational source may unify broad mathematical order and our capacity to grasp it beyond local adaptation.

name: Contingent reality and necessary concrete ground
conclusion: The ultimate explanatory basis includes necessary concrete reality; mind does not yet follow.
objection: Local explanations may exhaust the legitimate demand; necessary impersonal reality remains possible.
reply: Local causal links can leave why the totality obtains unanswered; exemptions from PSR need justification.

name: Fine-tuning comparative support
conclusion: E conditionally favors D over N; this alone establishes neither an overall posterior nor the full conscious-foundation package.
objection: Sensitivity does not fix a probability measure; a designer’s choice of laws and the evidential role of life are underdetermined.
reply: Qualitative orderings can matter without exact numbers; initial life may be evidence, and unexplained cause complexity need not erase a likelihood advantage.

name: Incremental stringency and divine indifference
position: conditional objection to a class of design arguments
conclusion: Under the matching assumptions, stringency adds no further design support once life is known.
objection: Divine and impersonal processes may justify different measures; ignorance alone is not uniformity.
reply: An argument relying on indifference must justify its asymmetric application; imposing matching distributions is an internal challenge, not an empirical law.

name: Physical time without a metaphysical shortcut
conclusion: These results do not establish a timeless conscious bearer.
objection: An all-history representation may naturally motivate eternalist ontology.
reply: Even eternalism contains earlier/later relations and does not identify a single experiencing mind.

name: A timeless conscious foundation with temporal manifestation
conclusion: Under these substantive assumptions M2 avoids the simple accumulation contradiction and could unify temporal order with conscious grounding.
objection: The model may redescribe history without explaining its concrete existence or subjective individuation; a fixed act may not count as agency.
reply: It posits an actual subject and reasons-guided dependence, rather than merely an abstract record; the absence of deliberation does not by definition exclude intention.

name: The tensed-knowledge challenge
conclusion: Then a cognitively perfect ground of this temporal world cannot meet H-T.
objection: A defender denies absolute presentness or argues one atemporal act knows every tensed fact through a non-successive access relation.
reply: The first response rejects a key premise and is a serious alternative; the second must explain access without either missing changing actuality or collapsing all times into one temporal present.

name: Timeless personhood and intentional responsiveness
conclusion: Simple personhood arguments do not automatically refute timelessness; actual interaction still needs a model.
objection: The proposed timeless capacities may be nominal; responsiveness to genuinely new events seems to require new states.
reply: Either justify whole-history reasons-sensitive dependence, or accept a temporal divine life with creation. Neither option is cost-free.

name: Whole-history preservation versus survival
conclusion: M3 inclusion alone supplies a preservation proposal, not H-S.
objection: An enlarged subject-history might include genuinely continuing subjectivity outside embodied succession.
reply: That is a distinct stronger hypothesis deserving assessment under an explicit identity relation; merely calling it inclusion does not establish it.

name: Identity and physical realization
conclusion: Physical identity/grounding is a live explanatory strategy, not disproved by epistemic difference alone.
objection: The account may capture reporting or causal role without phenomenal character.
reply: Identity theorist denies two items remain to be bridged once identity is warranted; separate epistemic access need not add a property.

name: Experiential bases and subject constitution
conclusion: Experiential bases could integrate phenomenality and causal roles without extra macro-level intervention.
objection: Microexperiences plus physics may not necessitate another subject; palette and structure constraints are distinct.
reply: The complete base can include phenomenal relations; informational rather than geometrical structure may matter. Inconceivability/impossibility is not established.

name: Naturalistic property dualism and causal/epistemic cost
position: PL1, with PL2 and substance variants differentiated
conclusion: A psychophysical-law model is a distinct serious alternative; it neither entails a separable person nor removes its epistemic burden.
objection: Under closure and no overdetermination, distinct experiential influence threatens exclusion; epiphenomenalism threatens experience-based knowledge/reporting.
reply: PL1 appeals to lawful tracking and direct acquaintance without extra physical effects; PL2 instead questions closure and proposes interaction laws. Neither reply is simply a conservation-law refutation.

name: Dissociated cosmic idealism
conclusion: The model offers a unified candidate explanation if dissociation, manifestation and law constraints are independently justified.
objection: An analogy to dissociation in embodied people does not establish cosmic subject division; calling brain activity an appearance can merely redescribe data.
reply: Distinguish inaccessible contents from nonexistent contents and causal impingement from shared cognitive access; formulate one lawful shared environment rather than personal wishing.

name: Cosmic constitution versus plural idealism
conclusion: Whole-first models relocate constitution rather than automatically solving it; plural idealism need not entail one universal subject.
objection: One subject cannot be numerically identical to multiple mutually distinct subjects under ordinary identity logic.
reply: Identity version relativizes access to modes; nonidentity version posits constitutive dependence. Plural idealism permits multiple basic subjects with lawful coordination.

name: Psychological appropriation and a repaired continuity criterion
conclusion: Such continuity is a candidate basis for same-person persistence.
objection: Memories may duplicate, disappear or presuppose ownership.
reply: Project repair: overlapping causal links and a nonbranching clause avoid direct-memory transitivity failure; they still need independent justification.

name: Thinking animal and biological persistence
conclusion: The human person is that organism; a disembodied copy alone does not preserve it.
objection: A transplanted cerebrum seems to carry the person; or the strict thinker is a soul/constituted subject.
reply: Olson presses costs of denying organism thought or multiplying thinkers; psychological evidence/concern may be mistaken for constitution.

name: Simple subject through qualitative change
conclusion: A soul is the candidate identity bearer.
objection: Epistemic underdetermination does not entail an immaterial entity; deny further-fact premise or specify a physical/causal identity rule.
reply: Charitable project reply: first-person numerical identity is not exhausted by descriptive similarity; the defender must argue that fact is real and immaterial, not merely unknowable.

name: Enlarged first-person history beyond bodily life
conclusion: M2 or enlargedM3 could satisfy H-S with foundation-level H-T.
objection: The asserted ownership/extension may restate survival; a universal knower can preserve a finite life without the person continuing.
reply: Treat subjectivity and individuation as substantive ontology with identifiable constraints; this blocks dismissal by definition but adds explanatory/evidential costs.

name: Temporal phenomenology under competing interpretations
conclusion: The reports motivate investigation but do not discriminate H-T/H-S without timing, identity and access evidence.
objection: Survival interpretation: coherent first-person reports and striking information may reveal real access beyond the body; instruments may miss their distinctiveness.
reply: Ordinary alternative has demonstrated drug-context overlap, while the survival reply correctly notes that inducing a resemblance need not explain a given case. Seek prospective, independently scored information and resolved timing; separately ask what identity relation it supports.

name: Enduring significance: necessity versus enhancement
conclusion: Endurance can enhance significance under these premises; necessity and actuality require more.
objection: Finite goods may retain value even when no one later remembers; endless continuation may damage what mattered.
reply: A defender can argue continued shared life is an additional relational good, not merely a record, while defending separately the stronger non-loss requirement.

name: Finite value with an acknowledged cosmic remainder
conclusion: Finite meaning can be real on this account while cosmic intention and enduring significance remain separate questions.
objection: A meaningful episode may still lack an ultimately worthwhile setting; all loss can defeat the hoped-for relationship to a larger whole.
reply: Distinguish missing further goods from nonexistence of prior goods; do not claim this answers the larger purpose question.

name: Williams on categorical desire and immortal life, with Fischer’s reply
position: Inspected original challenge and reply, with project adjudication
conclusion: Williams supplies a stronger challenge than mere hedonic boredom, but its universal necessity is not established by the present comparison; conditional worthwhile endurance remains open.
objection: Fischer allows varied activities, appropriately spaced repeatable pleasures, and acceptable character development; absorbed attention need not eliminate ownership. These contest inevitable exhaustion and indiscriminate identity-loss claims.
reply: A strengthened Williams-side response asks whether renewal preserves genuine engagement and prospective reasons rather than simply suppressing awareness of impoverishment. Occasional pleasantness does not settle that question, and every experience being owned does not by itself establish an adequate relation to present aims.

name: Cosmic purpose and normative worth
position: Strong purpose account with bridge audit
conclusion: A worthy intentional relation can add cosmic significance conditionally; observed conscious production alone does not establish it.
objection: Arbitrary or harmful ends would still be purposes; a timeless agent model owes coherent intention; designer premises remain unsupported.
reply: Specify a loving creator-person relation and whole-history intention, or temporal agency; assess these with the same standards as rival primitive laws and value commitments.

name: Consciousness-factory discrimination
conclusion: Precisely constrained variants can face qualitative tests; unrestricted hidden purposes discriminate weakly.
objection: Unknown goals/resources can accommodate almost any outcome; conscious observers necessarily observe from a conscious perspective.
reply: Precommit to independent goals, inclusion rules and feasible alternatives; compare the same data across intentional, impersonal-teleological and incidental models.

name: From conscious value to moral authority
conclusion: The full account could unify welfare, reasons, obligations and accountability if every bridge is warranted; consciousness alone proves none of the later bridges.
objection: Calling a being good or creative may presuppose the normativity being explained; unity and sanctions can yield only self-interest.
reply: Grounding need not be a definition or a temporal production: a defensible identity/constitution account can terminate explanation in a necessary good and a legitimate relation. This reply still owes warrant for that identity and relation.

name: Secular moral objectivity and its explanatory costs
position: Positive naturalistic account with other secular families retained
conclusion: A physicalist ontology has a substantive route to moral realism; this route remains contested and does not settle every categorical-reason demand.
objection: A fully informed egoist may still reject impartiality; reliable preference explanation might explain moral belief while omitting moral authority.
reply: Separate truth and applicability from the agent’s motivation; evaluate whether the proposed identity explains correction, practical criticism and disagreement. Other secular accounts can instead take categorical reasons or rational agency as basic, with their own costs.

name: Suffering as evidence against specified perfect governance
position: Evidential challenge, distinct from bare logical incompatibility
conclusion: Suffering challenges that attribute package if the evidential and normative premises hold; it is not a deduction from the mere occurrence of any evil.
objection: Our sample of goods, causal relations and feasible worlds may be too limited to assess what an omniscient being could justifiably permit.
reply: Finite limits do not automatically erase all evidence; compare what each hypothesis actually leads us to expect and what independently supports claimed limitations. Theistic countergrounds can rationally matter.

name: Restoration of persons and justification of harm
position: Strong enduring-restoration reply and victim-centered challenge
conclusion: Restoration can improve an account of what becomes of victims, while an account of why harms were permitted remains independently contestable.
objection: A later good may quiet grief without making the original injustice permissible; one person’s reconciliation cannot speak for another victim.
reply: The strongest version addresses each victim and distinguishes redemption from approval of wrongdoing; an internal consistency defense may use its own independently specified goods without claiming their actual existence is thereby proved.

name: Nonresistant nonbelief and relationship
position: Hiddenness challenge with a bounded, currently reconstructed reply
conclusion: If the premises hold, the specified perfectly loving personal God is excluded; other ultimate foundations remain open.
objection: Howard-Snyder distinguishes a desire for relationship now from an overriding reason to enable it now. Even a well-disposed inculpable seeker might benefit from owning or refining the disposition to love. He offers defeasible prima facie reasons and epistemic caution, not proof of actual divine reasons.
reply: Project comparison: a possible counterfactual disposition is not automatically resistance causing present nonbelief. Ask whether improving love can occur in an available relationship, and whether delaying access is no worse than other means once the lost relationship is counted. A defender may contest that comparison or our knowledge of it. Note18 and reply4 identify limits to this particular defense; no blanket victory is inferred.

name: Goodness, authority and dependence across the package
conclusion: This packet maps burdens for H-G and H-A, with conditional effects on H-I/P/S; it identifies neither a numerical posterior nor a winning full metaphysics.
objection: Restricting knowledge of unknown goods need not undermine simple moral knowledge; criticism can demand unreasonable omniscience of the defender.
reply: Use local rather than blanket skepticism and name what remains knowable; test whether the positive and negative inferences genuinely rely on the same inaccessible domain.

name: Dentures conditional anomalous-perception argument
conclusion: If the report and exclusion/timing premises hold, the specific neural-dependence model would be challenged.
objection: Single-witness retrospective timing and information control are insufficient to establish those premises.
reply: Unusual shelf details and pre-Thumper removal deserve testing; a generic ordinary possibility does not erase the report.

name: Reynolds conditional anomalous-perception argument
conclusion: If precise perception and independently established exclusion conditions coincide, the case favors acquisition beyond the specified normal channels.
objection: Checkable claims occur outside the alleged standstill interval, and drug/monitoring/access conditions are incompletely inspected.
reply: Carter’s technical details and visual specificity challenge simplistic hearing reconstructions; neither party has supplied the decisive controlled comparison here.

name: Limit of survival and cosmic extrapolation
conclusion: Neither dossier establishes the full enduring/timeless conscious-foundation package.
objection: A verified brain-independent episode could nevertheless be relevant to models permitting personal survival.
reply: Relevance is retained conditionally; irreversible death, numerical identity, universal subjecthood, purpose and normative relations require additional premises.

name: Causally generated nonstructural experience
conclusion: A causal-emergent model is available as a distinct proposal; its actuality is not established.
objection: The complete microphysical causal story might explain all effects; first-person access may not reveal hidden constitution.
reply: Specify emergents as intermediate causes; compare latent-powers alternatives fairly.

name: Noncausal-base causal preemption
conclusion: Emergent properties face causal and explanatory exclusion under the stated dependence assumptions.
objection: The base may act through an emergent causal intermediary, or mere necessitation may not bestow the relevant powers.
reply: The selected argument rules out a causal intermediary by its noncausal emergence premise; alternative dependence accounts need separate evaluation.

name: Temporal causal-chain reply
conclusion: Kim's selected preemption inference does not establish a contradiction in this revised model without its disputed premises.
objection: Relabeling the mechanism may add no explanatory benefit over latent microphysical powers.
reply: The authors contest simplicity and offer a history-dependent scenario; this motivates comparison without settling it.

name: Micro-latent powers and property individuation
position: Shoemaker countercase and reply to Kim
conclusion: A response to preemption can support a microstructural or descriptive account instead of basic nonstructural emergence.
objection: The individuation assumptions may be disputed; the 2005 model changes the dependence relation and contests the rival's simplicity.
reply: Shoemaker explicitly considers a causal-base option before rejecting it from his essential-powers commitments; the disagreement remains premise-dependent.

name: Lowe’s subject and intentional-causation model
conclusion: On those commitments, distinct subjects can explain intentional action while physical event chains remain complete.
objection: A physically sufficient event also fixes that it occurs; relabeling the intentional explanandum as a fact does not by itself remove competing sufficiency. Unity experienced in deciding does not independently settle causal event individuation.
reply: Lowe can challenge extension of event closure to facts and distinguish the type of intended outcome from its token realization. This works only with justified distinctions and counterfactuals.

name: Bennett’s conditional exclusion challenge
position: Nonreductive physicalist challenge to dualist compatibility
conclusion: A dualist with merely contingent psychophysical links needs a different response than the physicalist dependence strategy, unless a defensible necessitating relation is supplied.
objection: The decisive modal test may sever an explanatory embodiment relation and thereby test a different causal situation; metaphysical necessitation is not conceded to physicalism alone.
reply: A relation must explain the dependence and have independent motivation; arbitrary covariance cannot be stipulated into the fixed counterfactual background. Bennett also leaves completeness itself as a separate dualist dispute.

name: Engelhardt’s inclusive compatibility reply
position: Revised substance dualism with dependent property sharing
conclusion: A specified substance-dualist variant can contest the inference from two bearers to systematic independent overdetermination.
objection: Token sharing and embodiment may merely restate the dependence to be explained; if their modal force is unsupported, exclusion returns. A model that surrenders distinctive independent powers may not meet Lowe’s original explanatory ambition.
reply: Require a relation with explanatory standing comparable to relations accepted in physicalist constitution cases; do not assume numerical distinctness entails causal independence.

name: Reflective agency and the proposed authority of humanity
conclusion: If these bridges hold, reflective agents owe moral obligations that do not depend merely on contingent desires.
objection: A need for some reason or self-conception does not yet establish an impartial moral reason; public intelligibility may leave agent-relative authority intact.
reply: The proposed result is not an inference from private egoistic reasons to public ones; it challenges the assumed privacy and reconstructs principles constitutive of reflective agency.

name: Nagel’s direct challenge to law and identity grounding
position: Realist rival within the selected exchange
conclusion: The constructive account needs an additional justification of its law-like and interpersonal requirements, and may reverse the direction of normative explanation.
objection: Treating reflection as an already impersonal standpoint may assume the generality it seeks to justify; locating reasons in a standpoint does not alone settle whether they are discovered or constructed.
reply: Evaluate the actual reasons for treating persons’ interests as significant; moral concern need not be replaced by a self-image or payoff.

name: The constitutive reply and its explicit scope
conclusion: The reply offers formal universality and a response to reward-based interpretations; its full moral conclusion still depends on humanity and publicity arguments.
objection: Constitutive agency rules need independent defense; even granted general commitments, the all-persons domain and binding force of another’s reasons remain open.
reply: A rule internal to an activity need not be an arbitrary external command; the theory distinguishes genuine choice from impulse while retaining the content of concern for others.

name: Enoch’s indispensability strategy: introduction, partial book text and direct author reply
position: For justified belief in irreducible normative truth
conclusion: There is reason to believe irreducibly normative truths exist; a further moral bridge is needed.
objection: Lenman's thin/thick dilemma challenges joint satisfaction of both premises.
reply: Enoch distinguishes merited standards, first-person warrant and value-sensitive instrumental indispensability.

name: Lenman's schmeliberation countercase
conclusion: Robust truths have not been shown indispensable to unavoidable deliberation.
objection: Standards and similarity may not supply the deserved allegiance claimed necessary.
reply: Lenman regards stable concerns and critical reflection as sufficient without further ratification of the whole.

name: Enoch's direct reply to schmeliberation
conclusion: Lenman's alternative does not by itself remove Enoch's claimed reason to believe.
objection: Deserved allegiance may restate the disputed demand; private commitment needs a truth-directed epistemic bridge.
reply: Enoch invokes broader indispensability epistemology, permits premise error and distinguishes diminished projects from identical behavior.

name: Enoch’s conditional moral bridge
position: For extending justified general normative realism to robust moral realism, given moral objectivity
conclusion: On those assumptions, familiar alternatives to robust moral realism are under-motivated; other unconsidered motivations remain possible.
objection: Shared objections can impose continuing costs, moral and other normativity may differ in relevant respects, and the antecedent chapter3 case has not been fully checked. Naturalist or expressivist alternatives may have further motivations.
reply: Enoch contrasts accumulating costs with an objection defeated at the level of kind, and argues that moral objectivity requires normative privilege rather than mere etiquette. He expressly limits the result to a weak moral-reason link and an open-ended challenge.

name: Enoch’s qualified resistance to naturalist reduction
position: Defeasible initial suspicion of reduction with openness to successful detailed proposals
conclusion: Enoch retains suspicion but allows a strong specific, including token-level, reduction to overturn the initial commitment.
objection: The initial normative-force intuition may encode the disputed non-naturalism; the naturalist may accept concept difference while denying metaphysical difference.
reply: Enoch acknowledges this impasse and treats it as a limit on the argument, not a victory; he asks for detailed reductions capable of earning their theoretical costs and explicitly permits revising his intuition.

name: Agreed biological tests and conditional theory defense
position: Retain the tests as challenges, while distinguishing auxiliary assumptions from full-theory refutation.
conclusion: Preserve a consequential but conditional empirical challenge; neither a whole-theory winner nor automatic dismissal is warranted.
objection: Auxiliary-condition defenses can insulate a theory against agreed failed tests; the collaboration was explicitly negotiated to avoid that flexibility.
reply: The offset condition predates results publication, and the papers acknowledge measurement and implementation limits; nevertheless source attribution alone does not show that any proposed explanation accounts for the observed failures.

name: Document chronology and compliance are separate questions
position: Narrow the v1 methods gap without certifying preregistration compliance.
conclusion: Qualify the historical wording; retain unresolved full history and execution audit, and label exploratory analyses correctly.
objection: An internally inconsistent ordinary OSF node is insufficient evidence for a clean prospective analysis history.
reply: Agreed; the limited finding is the dated exact document and stated methods, not clean compliance. The matching 2024 copy does not erase the 2022 version record.

name: Do not substitute easier denominators
conclusion: Retain scoped causal/association constraints while withholding reconstructed rates, precision upgrades and population generalizations.
objection: Raw files or another appendix may contain the missing totals, so bounded non-recovery is not a source-level absence proof.
reply: The packet explicitly preserves that distinction and requests the exact missing table/data fields rather than inventing the counts.

name: Conditional experiential-ultimate argument
conclusion: Micropsychism, and panpsychism only with added homogeneity, conditional on the premises.
objection: Goff: the supposedly explanatory experiential base still needs unexplained subject and quality combination; no-radical-emergence may be an asymmetrically applied intuition.
reply: Strawson: same-kind experiential composition may be incomprehensible to us without the metaphysical impossibility he attributes to the wholly nonexperiential case.

name: Goff’s combination and revelation challenge
conclusion: The proposed panpsychism has not escaped brute emergence; under the stronger transparency/parthood assumptions novel experiential combination is incoherent.
objection: The transparency premise may exceed first-order acquaintance in certain respects; experiential constitution need not be additive or perspective-sharing.
reply: Goff: without sufficient transparency, Strawson must explain why ignorance does not equally protect physicalist reduction; footnote 2 extends the concern to experiential nature generally.

name: Partial acquaintance and active experiential constitution
conclusion: One full-revelation argument for impossibility can be resisted while experiential composition remains a conditional possibility requiring further account.
objection: The revised ontology and ignorance allowance do not explain composition and may weaken the original exclusion of nonexperiential emergence.
reply: Strawson acknowledges the concession, rejects exhaustive revelation in the relevant sense, and relies on a transcendental argument with smallism.

name: Equal explanatory standards and component limits
conclusion: Retain experiential constitution as a specified conditional alternative; withhold six-family ranking and all conclusion gates.
objection: A defender might regard no-radical-emergence and acquaintance as sufficiently decisive for actual panpsychism.
reply: The selected reply explicitly acknowledges intuitive premises, unknown composition and optional universal-subject extension.

name: EEG–recollection intersection challenge and direct reply
position: Critic and author exchange, with symmetric inference limits
conclusion: The main study does not establish the positive association, and the missing association does not establish that the EEG patterns cannot be consciousness markers.
objection: A plausible clinical EEG interpretation and implicit-memory analogy might support consciousness despite absent recall.
reply: These possibilities rebut a negative inference but do not identify the content or timing of an experience in the monitored participants.

name: From unusual recollection to extracerebral acquisition
position: Conditional favorable case and strongest methodological countercase
conclusion: Investigative interest remains warranted, but the inspected versions and correspondence do not establish excluded-process perception or brain independence.
objection: Author-checked resuscitation details and preserved cognition despite severe physiological compromise are difficult for simple absence-of-consciousness assumptions.
reply: Challenge to that simple assumption is not an exclusion of every brain-dependent account; subject-specific neural state, memory timing and ordinary information access remain unmeasured or unresolved.

name: Martial direct reply: explanatory limits and the fruit reference class
conclusion: The direct reply repairs debate coverage and offers a positive account; it does not close opportunity, timing, classification or guessing-model gaps.
objection: Clinical constraints and the rapidly changing state may make a stable-state critique inappropriate; standardized patterns and unusual responses may remain informative.
reply: Their information value must be assessed within the available measurements and protocol; neither lack of detailed analysis nor a noun-count denominator establishes the needed inference.

name: Cosmic dissociation as universal experiential grounding
conclusion: A one-primitive cosmic account can accommodate the selected phenomena.
objection: Chalmers: accessibility does not by itself establish subject constitution; identity has interpersonal/introspection costs and nonidentity needs necessitation.
reply: Kastrup’s clinical/privacy and appearance account makes the intended mechanism explicit; Chalmers himself grants cognitive-fragmentation coherence, with qualifications.

name: Conditional cosmic subject-constitution objection
conclusion: Pure cosmic grounding of distinct macrosubjects faces a serious conditional objection.
objection: Identity cosmopsychism denies further numerically distinct subjects; hidden constitutive facts or failure of modal bridges may defeat the inference.
reply: Chalmers allows mode-relative fragmentation as coherent but documents identity/introspection costs; nonidentity approaches still owe a subject relation.

name: Plural substantial unity and internally lawful representation
conclusion: Plural created perceivers express one world without forming one numerically identical subject.
objection: Foucher questions unextended foundations, organic/mental unity, and why externally coordinated bodies are needed if appearances are internally sufficient.
reply: Leibniz distinguishes genuine unities from aggregates and abstract extension from corporeal mass; intrinsic lawfulness and divine preference for plurality answer the intended explanandum.

name: Unnecessary bodies and post hoc coordination
conclusion: Leibniz owes justification for bodies and harmony beyond possible coordination.
objection: Leibniz says harmony follows from true unities, laws are internal, and God values more substances with external correspondence.
reply: Leibniz’s actual1696reply treats harmony as law-grounded rather than recurring intervention, permits revised ordinary causal language, and defends a priori reasons plus empirical fit.

name: Abductive case for a nonphenomenal account
conclusion: Frankish infers that phenomenal realism is mistaken and favors illusionism; his practical recommendation is to develop the programme. This attribution does not establish the abductive premises or the…
objection: A-P2T05-002 disputes that the target is exhausted by fallible representations and asks whether the economy argument starts from a distorted target.
reply: A-P2T05-003 contests whether ostension fixes the target’s realist nature and returns the burden to an account of unmediated awareness.

name: Experiential target, reference and immediate awareness
conclusion: Given the stated exemplification and target premises, denial of experiential consciousness fails; the argument is conditional, as her§4 explicitly says.
objection: A-P2T05-003 accepts the examples and commonality but disputes that they rule out a nonphenomenal interpretation; rejecting PPP alone cannot block a recast illusionist claim.
reply: Her§2 p7 supplies the immediate-awareness argument, and§3 p9 distinguishes misdescribing a real property from denying its instantiation. These address more than a bare assertion that consciousness exists.

name: Reply: reference need not settle nature
position: Frankish’s actual response to the selected critic
conclusion: Reference fixing alone does not rule out his illusionist ontology; the remaining immediate-awareness disagreement reaches explicitly acknowledged metaphysical commitments.
objection: Nida-Rümelin’s positive awareness premise targets B-P2T05-05/06: preserving verbal examples need not preserve the experiential property she points to.
reply: He does not merely deny the examples: he specifies an alternative account of their commonality. His physicalist refusal of robust acquaintance is candidly qualified as unpersuasive to this critic.

name: Illusion, regress and the remaining content burden
position: Strong sourced challenge and the selected author’s replies
conclusion: The regress objection identifies a real explanatory constraint; it is not automatically a contradiction once functional seeming and limited introspection are allowed.
objection: Merely renaming a state a nonphenomenal representation does not explain why it presents determinate apparent qualities or captures what the critic means by experience.
reply: Original§§3.2–3.4 rejects phenomenal content vehicles and inner observers; reply pp9–10 allows a limited higher-order route; p23 allows fine-grained nonphenomenal states. None is claimed as a completed mechanism.

name: From possible explanation to actual explanation of the maximal contingent fact
conclusion: Conditionally, the actual BCCF has an actual explanation.
objection: Oppy: universal W-PSR entails the strong principle under explanatory assumptions; weaker counterpart intuitions do not warrant the world-complete premise, and informed rational dissent can remain.
reply: The actual2002 reply grants the deduction while defending epistemic plausibility, incomplete deductive understanding, and a preference for explanation over brute facts; it offers a conditional restricted BCCF* fallback (pp90–97).

name: From total explanation to a necessary free agent and its attributes
conclusion: Conditionally, a necessary free agent creates the actual universe; rich qualities require further arguments.
objection: The defender’s reported Quinn alternative is an impersonal indeterministic necessary source; the strongest project question is why libertarian self-explanation is sufficient when impersonal indeterminism is not, given context-sensitive explanatory fullness.
reply: Gale and Pruss argue that only free action can be an indeterministic self-explainer, appeal to cosmic order, and offer a generic necessary powerful cause fallback (p472).

name: Weak-to-strong PSR and informed rejection
conclusion: The advertised weakness advantage is not established by those premises; rational rejection can remain.
objection: The2002 reply grants entailment but argues that incomplete deductive knowledge can coexist with adequate understanding, that evil does not defeat every necessary creator, and that W-PSR better coheres with inquiry (pp90–97).
reply: Oppy conditions the objection on independent rational grounds and distinguishes modal intuition about a duplicate from the universal world-complete premise; he does not prove all non-theists possess the needed grounds.

name: Lennox’s compatibility and positive order argument
position: Selected Lennox relevance, not a direct reply to Gale–Pruss or Oppy
conclusion: The essay supplies a compatible creator interpretation and a further positive abductive claim; its comparative strength remains unresolved.
objection: Artifact analogy and asserted creator preferences do not independently establish a cosmic designer or show natural cognition unreliable.
reply: Lennox explicitly offers positive intelligibility and sophistication reasons, not only compatibility; excluding all non-scientific explanation would itself need argument.

name: Participant-specific defeat and the justice objection
position: Developed Adams internal-coherence defense; serious direct Sutherland criticism and limited revised-response dossier
conclusion: Adams argues for conditional internal compatibility; actual restoration and adequate original permission are not established here.
objection: Sutherland pp318–323: eventual reassurance does not decide justice of the original treatment or settle other victims’ claims; moral perception may be distorted.
reply: Revised Adams reproduction PDF2,5–6 explicitly affirms objective scope, gives a reason for whole-life value, and denies that defeat erases injustice or undermines moral judgment. This answers a claimed entailment, not every permission burden.

name: Temporary nonbelief for ownership and fittingness of love
position: Howard-Snyder defense tested by Schellenberg’s actual1996 response
conclusion: A qualified challenge to confidence that no reason for temporary nonbelief exists; not an explanation of every actual nonbeliever or cultural distribution.
objection: Schellenberg pp460–462: development, confirmation and choosing continuation may occur after belief with additional benefits; no-worse comparative premise and human-lover analogy are challenged.
reply: Howard-Snyder’s earlier internal replies pp448–451 distinguish ownership from fittingness, improvement from perfection and prima facie from conclusive reasons; p453 offers an epistemic fallback. These are available defenses already in the1996article, NOT a later reply to Schellenberg1996. No such later rebuttal inspected.

name: Positive support for divine intention versus an independent no-reason premise
position: Schellenberg’s structural reply and the surviving epistemic dispute
conclusion: The target of Howard-Snyder’s fallback depends on which argument is defended; no full positive case or metaphysical conclusion is established by this distinction alone.
objection: Howard-Snyder pp433–439,453: desire for access does not by itself show an all-things-considered intention; inaccessible reasons may remain.
reply: Schellenberg pp457–459 appeals to positive support, accepts defeaters and the negative existential commitment, but rejects requiring an independent Rowe-style inference.

name: Final loss and the necessity of endurance
position: Reconstructed strict necessity rationale; neither Yoshizawa nor Metz endorses its soundness
conclusion: The third premise would require endurance for meaning only if the loss-to-meaninglessness bridge is defended.
objection: Yoshizawa distinguishes no existing subject from an existing subject without meaning, and past meaning from present instantiation; strict necessity does not follow from an ending.
reply: Metz reformulates the strict rationale to avoid conceding finite meaning, then questions whether endless retention avoids ideal value; his hypothetical further response separates perfection from explanatory work.

name: Possible worthwhile continuation with ownership and engagement
conclusion: A coherent worthwhile continuation may enhance a life, while finite meaning and actual survival remain separate questions.
objection: Williams’s stronger concern is exhausted categorical projects or a remote life not appropriately related to the present person; ordinary repetition may fail indefinitely.
reply: Fischer distinguishes repeatable from self-exhausting goods, permits a varied life and appropriate character changes, and separates absorption from ownership.

name: Finite value, ultimate context and intended purpose
position: Several conditional questions; no forced metaphysical winner
conclusion: Finite value and possible divine/enduring enhancement can be compared without deriving purpose, perfect goodness or actual continuation.
objection: An advocate may argue all finite value requires divine grounding or that ultimate loss defeats local significance.
reply: Wolf identifies finite fitting engagement but expressly limits cosmic solace; Metz concedes limited force of his timeless-purpose challenge in the 2015 selectedpassage. The 2000 original itself already leaves two response strategies open and does not claim the objection requires disbelief (p311).

name: Collins conditional comparative route with explicit version limits
conclusion: Conditional comparative support, not final theism or a verified designer.
objection: Observation selection and unestablished measures/preferences; moving from a finite illuminated comparison to an all-reality conclusion needs care.
reply: Collins restates existence evidence and defends epistemic probability; Sober grants a trace inequality but disputes which conditioned observation is relevant.

name: White–Weisberg direct probability disagreement
conclusion: Added stringency support follows conditionally; third-premise rationale remains contested.
objection: Weisberg’s judge counterexample and matched distributions undermine the no-known-preference rationale.
reply: White shows low absolute designer likelihood does not negate a comparative advantage; Dorst later supplies a distinct stringency-class weighting.

name: Dorst mixture extension and its residual model dependence
conclusion: Conditional positive support can survive uncertainty and some deviations from exact indifference.
objection: The supplied McCutcheon manuscript adds uncertainty over the laxity range; under its uniform hyperprior the claimed giant ratio falls to about 61, and under a family of power priors it becomes approximately neutral in a limit. Thus a tiny sufficient mixture weight is not secured by indifference uncertainty alone.
reply: The actual 2022 reply includes Else and defends a lower bound and sensitivity to departures preserving likelihood separation. That sufficient condition remains valid. A defense of a fixed range or a different proper hyperprior would require further justification; this is a researcher-identified possible response, not an actual reply to the 2026 manuscript.

name: Sober time-indexed observation-selection critique
conclusion: The selected observation need not discriminate between ID and Chance despite an unconditioned trace inequality.
objection: The conditioning basis is disputed and compatibility is not the same datum as learned stringency; firing-squad analogy requires separate chronology.
reply: Sober revises the firing-squad verdict while preserving earlier-life conditioning for stable constants; rejects an indiscriminate recipe against all design evidence.

name: Range uncertainty challenges the scale of the mixture advantage
conclusion: The extreme fixed-range ratio is sensitive to additional range uncertainty. The broad conclusion of universal evidential neutrality is not established.
objection: The hyperprior and interpretation of x are additional assumptions. The uniform example retains positive support; the exact improper endpoint is unavailable, and neglected small terms can determine the sign near neutrality.
reply: The manuscript motivates uncertainty over x and a multiplicative independent-hoops prior; its proper finite-p examples already erode the enormous ratio without needing an improper endpoint. These are actual manuscript replies to its uniform-prior limitation, not a later response from Dorst.

name: Eternal life with temporal effects and direct presence
conclusion: If those premises and bridges hold, an eternal agent can be cognitively/causally related to temporal persons without itself undergoing their succession.
objection: Lewis1984P/causal actuality and1988existential-presence/tense arguments challenge whether the proposed relation can be actual or coherent, rather than merely named.
reply: S&K1992argue against shared-mode requirements via nonspatial divine presence and make causal/awareness capacity explicit inET′.

name: The presentness objection and the exact later reply
position: Serious critic/reply assessment with version boundaries
conclusion: Under those premises the1981account either misses present actuality or commits to a tenseless ontology; the selected1992reply contests cross-mode premises but does not conclusively settle the tense d…
objection: Defenders can challenge the necessity of shared mode and reject the critic’s assumed temporal-to-eternal transfer; temporalism is not established merely by insisting on it.
reply: Lewis’s strongest1988case appeals to the metaphysical price of spatial analogies; S&Kacknowledge the absolute-present mismatch. Its additional moral argument is now separately examined as Lewis1986→Oaklander1987–88 in A-P2T12-004.

name: Eternal relation does not entail human survival or identity
conclusion: The selected exchange cannot by itself establish enduring human consciousness, postmortem survival or a solution to branching/continuity; divine personhood and human identity remain distinct.
objection: A broader dualist, resurrection or constitution theory might add a same-bearer relation and a reason to expect continued experience.
reply: That would require its own defended premises and exact source evidence. P2T02was accepted only as a bounded derivative comparator and does not supply automatic survival.

name: Tenseless human persons, persistence and responsibility
position: Developed human-identity objection and actual direct reply
conclusion: The claimed necessary incompatibility of tenselessness with human moral agency is contested by explicit alternatives; the exchange supplies no general evidential identity criterion, postmortem contin…
objection: Lewis argues beyond stage nonidentity: a momentary stage cannot span an action, while a temporal whole allegedly has no consciousness, intentions or bodily members; a responsibility bearer must be more than a collection of events.
reply: Oaklander distinguishes tenseless continuants without parts, the whole referenced through different stages, and psychological/physical continuity; the ordinary sameness condition does not alone entail a simple substance. His reply attacks the claimed necessity rather than settling every metaphysical account.

name: Alexander’s conditional cortical-exclusion and veridical-detail argument
position: Strongest developed defender, reconstructed without endorsing premises
conclusion: Conditional pressure on a specified brain-production account; unconditional survival/creator conclusion not established.
objection: A-P2T15-002: timing, residual/recovering function and information-access bridges are unverified.
reply: AppendixB and Mays appeal to severity, elaborate interactive recall, recovery phenomenological contrast and corroborative testimony; these deserve inspection.

name: Underdetermination of cause and time
position: Serious direct criticism plus author audit of evidence limits
conclusion: Specific ordinary and nonordinary causes remain underdetermined.
objection: A-P2T15-001: exceptionally severe impairment and matching details might challenge ordinary production if independently established.
reply: Retain those positive reports, distinguish absence of accessible evidence from evidence of absence, and state exactly which timing/function/acquisition tests remain unmet.

name: Mays’s actual reply to a solely pharmacological account
position: Narrow direct reply with later clinical comparison
conclusion: Drug-only dismissal is unsupported by this packet; rejecting it does not prove a cortex-free experience.
objection: Potter statement is mediated, removed at request, and unsupported by original tape; memoir timing/clinical figures differ.
reply: Wade’s separately signed account and published record-review account strengthen illness attribution but retain the causal/timing limits.

name: Conditional Reynolds anomalous-perception argument
position: Strongest selected positive case; project reconstruction
conclusion: Visual specificity and the disputed monitoring/hearing setup motivate investigation, but this packet does not establish excluded-process acquisition.
objection: Early checkable phases are not the absent-brainstem/arrest interval; retrospective report and incomplete information controls allow ordinary hearing/reconstruction alternatives.
reply: The later technical details, conscious-hearing distinction and missing click reports challenge an unqualified assertion that ordinary hearing has been demonstrated.

name: Conditional ordinary-process account and its correction
position: Strongest selected direct critic and actual replies
conclusion: The ordinary-process account remains a live alternative; Woerlee’s rejoinder narrows the evidential conclusion and does not exclude the rival.
objection: Carter/Smit contest acoustic equivalence, subjective character and inferential moves from monitoring/marginal symptoms.
reply: Woerlee distinguishes bone from air conduction and acknowledges BAER is not conscious hearing; Smit’s own reported results include some hearing. Neither decides the case mechanism.

name: Demonstration, dependence and extrapolation limits
conclusion: The packet can revise source/reply coverage and technical attributions while leaving all twelve stronger-conclusion gates withheld.
objection: A well-established anomaly could still be relevant to models permitting survival.
reply: Conditional relevance is preserved; timing, identity, persistence and cosmic/normative bridges require additional evidence.

name: Vivid continuity and the reported Nelson–Barker exchange
position: Strongest conditional positive case with directly case-linked criticism and actual third-party reply
conclusion: The positive case is worth exact documentation; the present packet supports attributed experience and a conditional argument, not survival.
objection: Nelson’s reported distinction separates vivid memory from interpretation; REM intrusion/hypoxia is a possible alternative. Unknown timing and later information exposure undermine a uniquely survival-based inference.
reply: Barker’s actual reply grants that brain states might be present yet argues correlates need not determine interpretation; first-person quality deserves consideration. This blocks an automatic dismissal but supplies no missing Neal measurements.

name: Rescue interval and clinical inference
conclusion: Retain testimony and reported recovery; withhold a synchronized medical reconstruction and specific process exclusion.
objection: Neal identifies rescue-trained Long family members and reports listening to each individually, while the book gives a watch range and substantial injury detail. Those specific reports deserve assessment and could guide public corroboration.
reply: The actual versions differ in timing and start events; no original timekeeper account resolves them. Specific testimony is not a synchronized physiological record. Later reported saturation or no-injury assertions do not date river awareness to absent neural function.

name: Prediction, fulfillment and prior documentation
conclusion: Retain attributed prediction and documented reporting chronology; withhold verified foreknowledge and odds.
objection: The strongest countercase to a successful-prediction reading combines postevent access to all detailed accounts, missing predated wording/scoring, internally different manuscript labels, and the separate age-specific child prediction followed by a changed-plan interpretation. Unknown counts prevent a rate calculation in either direction.
reply: Neal reports early confidants and a manuscript before learning of the death, and interprets some foreknowledge as involving changeable plans. These are meaningful positive claims to preserve, but presently only retrospective; a flexible-plan reply needs a prior scoring rule to establish predictive accuracy.

name: Conditional unusual-cart and pre-Thumper argument
position: Strongest bounded extracerebral-perception case reconstructed from defenders
conclusion: Potential case-specific challenge conditional on premises; no established brain-independent perception.
objection: The report depends on one retrospective witness and unmeasured timing; the original pump-first passage and drawer-word reply problem remain.
reply: TG explicitly corrects the pump sequence and defenders reject the specific noisy-metal-drawer mechanism. A generic appeal to hearing does not itself explain every unusual detail.

name: Ordinary awareness and reconstruction account with direct replies
position: Strong serious countercase, not asserted causal resolution
conclusion: Ordinary processes remain live; their complete causal adequacy for this event remains unresolved.
objection: TG’s reply denies pump operation at removal and describes a pre-opened wooden shelf; generic physiology is not this patient’s data.
reply: The reply remains retrospective and does not replace the earlier wording or supply a measured neural interval. The critic need not prove a mechanism to challenge an assertion of impossibility.

name: Dependency and nine-component boundary
conclusion: Append source/version and chronology qualifications to C-T19-001 while retaining all twelve gates and nine component distinctions.
objection: A credible detailed witness report can still have evidential value without being a prospective target experiment.
reply: The packet retains that conditional value and the specific cart challenge while declining unsupported extrapolations.

name: Historical recurrence and the prospective report: strongest bounded positive case
position: Conditional relevance to an experiential phenomenon and to better tests of H-B
conclusion: This selected corpus and pilot justify investigating recurring reported experiences, without establishing a unique cause, global recurrence rate or brain independence.
objection: European literary/reporting dependence, unmeasured historical danger states, selected survivors, unknown target opportunities and bodily-awareness coding can generate misleading convergence.
reply: Those limitations do not erase the dated reports or show every account was fabricated or normally explained. A constrained hypothesis can still seek evidence that alternatives predict differently.

name: Controlled-target countercase and actual exchange
position: Challenges overinterpretation of veridicality evidence; does not establish a physicalist winner
conclusion: The selected Parnia reports provide no validated concealed-target success and no verified effective-trial denominator. Neither the target null nor the unresolved ordinary-route alternatives settle th…
objection: Greyson argues that untested error possibilities should not outweigh reports and cited stability evidence; he disputes Augustine’s treatment of paranormal-feature stability and default priors.
reply: Augustine concedes possibility is not actuality and small target numbers are inconclusive, but demands evidence excluding ordinary information routes. The project accepts that evidential requirement without adopting his unmeasured causal verdict or twelve-case denominator.

name: Measurement and dependence countercase
position: Limits pooled cultural and prospective convergence
conclusion: Use a nonadditive, source-qualified comparison; preserve all old numbers and unknowns while adding exact reuse and wording qualifications.
objection: Recurring motifs across times and conditions may reflect a common phenomenon even when instruments differ; documenting dependence is not a causal explanation of every case.
reply: That possibility remains. Distinctive support requires comparable ascertainment and predictions that survive the stated coding/overlap uncertainties. Neither cultural nor neural mechanisms are established by bookkeeping.
